Madame and Mademoiselle L’Espanaye were not killed by spirits. Those responsible were physical beings, and they escaped by physical means. How, then? Fortunately, there is only one way to reason through this question, and it must bring us to a definite conclusion. Let us consider the possible exits one at a time. Clearly, the killers were in the room where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye was found, or at least in the adjoining room, when the group came upstairs. We therefore need to look for exits only from these two rooms. The police have exposed the floors, ceilings, and brickwork of the walls in every direction. No concealed exit could have escaped their scrutiny. But rather than rely on their eyes, I used my own to examine the place. There were, then, no concealed exits. Both doors opening from the rooms into the hallway were firmly locked, with the keys on the inside. Let us consider the chimneys. Although they remain a normal width for eight or ten feet above the fireplaces, farther along they would not allow even a large cat to pass through. Since escape by any of the means already considered is absolutely impossible, we are left with the windows. No one could have escaped through the front room’s windows without being seen by the crowd in the street. The murderers must therefore have gone through those in the back room. Having reached this conclusion so unmistakably, we cannot, as reasoning people, discard it because of apparent impossibilities. All that remains is to show that these apparent ‘impossibilities’ are not actually impossible.

“There are two windows in the bedroom. No furniture blocks one of them, and it is entirely visible. The bottom part of the other is concealed by the head of the cumbersome bedstead, which has been pushed right against it. The first was found securely fastened from inside. Those who tried to raise it used all their strength without success. A large hole had been drilled into the left side of its frame, and a very thick nail was found inserted there almost up to its head. When the other window was examined, a similar nail was found fitted in the same way; a forceful attempt to raise that sash also failed. The police were now completely convinced that no one had escaped in either direction. Consequently, they thought removing the nails and opening the windows would be unnecessary trouble.

“My own examination was rather more thorough, for the reason I have just explained: I knew this was the place where every apparent impossibility had to be shown, in reality, to be nothing of the kind.

Suddenly Mr. Podgers let go of Lord Arthur’s right hand and grabbed his left. He bent so close to examine it that the gold rims of his glasses almost touched the palm. For a moment his face turned white with horror, but he soon regained his composure. Looking up at Lady Windermere with a strained smile, he said, ‘It is the hand of a charming young man.’

‘Of course it is!’ Lady Windermere replied. ‘But will he be a charming husband? That is what I want to know.’

‘All charming young men are,’ said Mr. Podgers.

‘I don’t think a husband ought to be too attractive,’ Lady Jedburgh murmured thoughtfully. ‘It is so dangerous.’

‘My dear child, they never are too attractive,’ Lady Windermere exclaimed. ‘But I want details. Details are the only interesting things. What is going to happen to Lord Arthur?’

‘Well, in the next few months Lord Arthur will take a voyage—’

‘Oh yes, his honeymoon, of course!’

‘And lose a relative.’

‘Not his sister, I hope?’ said Lady Jedburgh in a distressed voice.

‘Certainly not his sister,’ Mr. Podgers replied, waving away the suggestion. ‘Only a distant relative.’

‘Well, I am terribly disappointed,’ said Lady Windermere. ‘I have absolutely nothing to tell Sybil tomorrow. No one cares about distant relatives these days. They went out of fashion years ago. Still, I suppose she should keep a black silk dress handy; it is always suitable for church, you know. Now let us go to supper. They are sure to have eaten everything, but we may find some hot soup. François used to make excellent soup, but politics has him so upset at present that I can never quite trust him. I do wish General Boulanger would keep quiet. Duchess, surely you must be tired?’

‘Not at all, dear Gladys,’ the Duchess answered, waddling toward the door. ‘I have enjoyed myself enormously, and the foot doctor—I mean the palm reader—is most interesting. Flora, where can my tortoiseshell fan be? Oh, thank you so much, Sir Thomas. And my lace shawl, Flora? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, how very kind’; and the good lady finally managed to get downstairs without dropping her perfume bottle more than twice.

Throughout all this, Lord Arthur Savile had stood beside the fireplace, still gripped by dread and the same sickening feeling that something terrible was coming. He smiled sadly at his sister as she swept past on Lord Plymdale’s arm, looking lovely in her pink brocade and pearls. He barely heard Lady Windermere call for him to follow her. His thoughts turned to Sybil Merton, and the possibility that anything might come between them filled his eyes with tears.

She studied me intently for a little while, then said quietly,

“What do you want for them?”

“Only,” I said, “that you shouldn’t confuse them with the others. They may share the same blood, but believe me, they do not share the same nature.”

Still watching me closely, Miss Havisham repeated,

“What do you want for them?”

“As you can see, I’m not clever enough,” I answered, aware of a slight blush, “to hide from you that I do want something, even if I wished to. Miss Havisham, if you could spare the money to give my friend Herbert some lasting help in life—help which, under the circumstances, he must know nothing about—I could show you how.”

“Why must he know nothing about it?” she asked, resting her hands on her stick so that she could study me more attentively.

“Because,” I said, “I began helping him myself more than two years ago, without his knowing, and I don’t want my involvement revealed. I cannot explain why I’m no longer able to finish what I began. That belongs to a secret which is someone else’s, not mine.”

Her eyes slowly moved away from me and turned toward the fire. She watched it for what seemed, in the silence and the light of the slowly burning candles, a long time. The collapse of some glowing coals stirred her, and she looked at me again, at first blankly, then with her attention gradually coming into focus. Estella continued knitting throughout. Once Miss Havisham had fixed her attention on me, she spoke as though there had been no pause in our conversation.

“What else?”

“Estella,” I said, turning to her now and trying to steady my trembling voice, “you know I love you. You know how long and how deeply I have loved you.”

At these words she lifted her eyes to my face. Her fingers continued their work, and she watched me with an unchanged expression. I noticed Miss Havisham looking from me to her, then from her back to me.

“I would have said this sooner if I hadn’t been mistaken for so long. My mistake led me to hope that Miss Havisham intended us for each other. While I believed that you had, in a sense, no choice in the matter, I held back from saying it. But now I must.”

Her expression still unchanged and her fingers still moving, Estella shook her head.

“I know,” I said in response to that movement. “I know. I have no hope that I will ever call you mine, Estella.
